guide.title: Medical, Legal & Ethical Issues
guide.lead: Most legal trouble in EMS comes from three things: not caring for someone you had a duty to, care below the standard, and careless records or talk. Know the elements of negligence, protect privacy, report what the law requires, and when principles collide, act in the patient's interest and call medical direction.

sections.title: Negligence: all four must be proved
rows: You had an obligation to care (on duty, or once you started)
You fell below the standard of care

sections.title: Terms to know
rows: Ending care without handing over to an equal or higher provider
Moving or holding a capable person against their will
Protect off-duty helpers who act in good faith, within their training, without payment and without gross negligence

sections.title: Confidentiality

groups.title: Share with
items: Whoever the law requires (courts, mandatory reports)

groups.title: Never
items: Talk in public – even without names if the patient could be identified

notes: Laws differ (HIPAA in the US, GDPR in Europe); the principle is the same.

sections.title: Must report (varies by jurisdiction)
items: Abuse of older or vulnerable adults
Gunshot and stab wounds in many places

steps.title: Safe first
steps.text: Police secure the scene before you enter.

steps.title: Patient care comes first
steps.text: But touch only what you need, and use one path in and out.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.text: Cut around bullet and knife holes; put clothing in separate paper bags; don't move weapons unless needed for safety.

steps.title: Document
steps.text: What you moved, where, and who you handed things to.

sections.title: Four ethical principles
rows: Act in the patient's best interest
Treat everyone fairly, whatever their race, money or status
notes: A capable patient refusing care for a heart attack is autonomy against beneficence.

sections.title: End of life
items: Valid out-of-hospital DNR: no CPR; give comfort care, even if family asks for more
Living will alone (no DNR or POLST): start CPR and call medical direction, per local law
DNR mentioned but not produced: start care; document your attempts to find it
Organ donor: resuscitate exactly as you would anyone else

quiz.q: Scope of practice is best defined as:
options: The range of duties authorised by law and medical direction
What a reasonable provider would do
quiz.explanation: Standard of care is what a reasonable provider would do.

quiz.q: To prove negligence, a plaintiff does NOT need to show:
Off duty, a shopper collapses. Good Samaritan protection does NOT cover:
options: A procedure you are not trained for
quiz.explanation: Gross negligence and acts beyond your training aren't protected.

quiz.q: Discussing a patient in a restaurant without using the name is:
options: A privacy breach if the patient could be identified

quiz.q: Which usually does NOT have to be reported?
options: A patient who stopped taking blood pressure tablets
Unexplained bruising in an older adult
quiz.explanation: Reporting rules vary; abuse and violence are the usual ones.

quiz.q: Cardiac arrest with a valid out-of-hospital DNR; the family begs you to 'do something'. You:
options: Follow the DNR and give comfort care
Call medical direction for permission to resuscitate
Start and sort out the paperwork later
quiz.explanation: Support the family; the patient's wishes stand.

quiz.q: Refusing to treat a patient because of their race violates:
You must cut a shirt with a bullet hole. Best approach?
A registered organ donor is in cardiac arrest. You:
options: Resuscitate exactly as for anyone else
Go only to a transplant centre
Call medical direction before any care
quiz.explanation: Donor status never changes your care.

quiz.q: Cardiac arrest; the spouse shows a living will saying 'no heroic measures' but there is no DNR. You:
options: Start CPR and contact medical direction
Start CPR and never call anyone
Phone the family doctor before acting
quiz.explanation: A living will is not a DNR order in most places.

quiz.q: A parent refuses to let you assess a child you suspect is being abused. True statement:
options: Call police and document what you saw and heard
Implied consent lets you examine the child against the parent's wishes
quiz.explanation: Police can act to protect the child; report the concern.

quiz.q: Which is a conflict between autonomy and beneficence?
options: A capable patient with a likely heart attack refuses transport
Family wants CPR despite a valid DNR
Choosing between patients at a mass casualty
quiz.explanation: Respect the choice; keep trying to persuade; document.

flashcards.question: Scope of practice vs standard of care
flashcards.answer: Scope: what the law and your medical director allow. Standard: what a reasonable provider with your training would do in the same situation.

flashcards.question: Four elements of negligence
flashcards.answer: Duty, breach, damages, causation. All four must be proved.

flashcards.question: Good Samaritan protection
flashcards.answer: Good faith, within your training, no payment, no gross negligence. Mostly for off-duty help.

flashcards.question: Mandatory reports
flashcards.answer: Child abuse, abuse of older or vulnerable adults, certain infections, often gunshot and stab wounds, animal bites, some crimes – per local law.

flashcards.question: Four ethical principles
flashcards.answer: Autonomy, beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (do no harm), justice (fairness).

flashcards.question: Family says there's a DNR but can't find it
flashcards.answer: Start resuscitation and contact medical direction. Document your attempts to find it.

flashcards.question: Crime scene priorities
flashcards.answer: Scene safety first (police), then patient care, then evidence: touch little, cut around holes, paper bags, document what you moved.

flashcards.question: Patient privacy
flashcards.answer: Share only with those caring for the patient, billing, quality review or as the law requires. Breaches bring fines, dismissal and, for deliberate misuse, criminal charges (HIPAA, GDPR and others).

critical.scenario: Police have secured a home: a woman with a gunshot wound to the lower abdomen, weak radial pulse. You need to expose the wound. She begs: 'Don't tell my husband I was here with someone else.'
critical.question: How do you balance care, evidence and confidentiality?

options.t: Cut around the bullet hole, bag the clothing, give full care, document; explain that you'll share only what her care and the law require
Transport fully clothed to preserve evidence
Cut through the hole and promise total secrecy
options.f: You can't promise that, and evidence is lost.

options.t: Wait for police photos before care

critical.explanation: Her personal life isn't yours to share with her husband.
critical.kpi: Balances patient care, evidence preservation and confidentiality

critical.scenario: Nursing home: 82-year-old, fever, RR 28, SpO₂ 88%. Staff say there's a DNR but can't find it. His daughter says 'no oxygen, no hospital'; his son says 'do everything – DNR means no CPR only'.
critical.question: Best course?

options.t: Oxygen and transport; explain that a DNR covers CPR only and can't be confirmed; withhold CPR only if a valid DNR is produced
Follow the daughter and withhold care
options.f: A DNR isn't 'do not treat', and it isn't confirmed.

options.t: Ask medical direction whether to ignore the DNR
options.f: You can contact them, but treat first.

critical.explanation: Contact medical direction if the family conflict continues.

critical.scenario: A 19-year-old took pills after a break-up; now awake. She begs you not to tell her strict parents, who are waiting at the hospital.
critical.question: How do you handle confidentiality?

options.t: Tell her you must give the hospital the full facts for her safety, document accurately, and leave what is shared with her parents to the hospital team
Tell her parents it was food poisoning
Ask police to inform the parents
Leave the overdose out of the report
options.f: Falsifying records is illegal and unsafe.

critical.explanation: Don't discuss details with family yourself; suicide risk needs full assessment.
critical.kpi: Maintains confidentiality while ensuring accurate clinical handover
